quote: In relative terms, StoneDB's bulk-insert throughput was about 54 percent higher than KVLite's.
problem: Arithmetic error: A2 gives 348 vs 212, and 348/212 = 1.64, so about 64 percent higher, not 54.

quote: Marlin's higher write throughput comes from its batched write-ahead log, which groups concurrent writes into a single append.
problem: Causal claim unsupported. The README only describes the write path; A1 says no profiler, tracing or ablation runs were collected, so the benchmark cannot attribute the speed to the batched WAL.

quote: Marlin's write advantage holds regardless of storage hardware or durability settings.
problem: Overgeneralisation. All results come from one machine (NVMe SSD, Linux 6.1) and one log-sync setting (fsync every 1,000 writes for all stores); per-write fsync was not tested and no other hardware was used.

quote: Marlin also serves random reads faster than StoneDB.
problem: Overstated. A2 workload B: Marlin 417 [391-426] vs StoneDB 402 [395-410]. The ranges overlap and the 15K median gap is small with 5 runs, so the difference is not established.

quote: Under the mixed workload, KVLite's median p99 latency was 4.2 ms, the worst of the three, against 3.1 ms for StoneDB and 2.9 ms for Marlin.
problem: Wrong figure: A3 gives KVLite's median p99 as 4.8 ms [4.5-5.2], not 4.2 ms. The StoneDB and Marlin figures and the ranking are correct.

quote: StoneDB sustains its mixed-workload throughput over long-running operation.
problem: Unsupported. The longest run was 6 minutes (workload C including warm-up) and no soak or multi-hour run was done. A5 shows only five measured minutes, so long-running behaviour was not tested.

quote: As for what the projects say about themselves, Marlin's own documentation presents it as the right engine for write-intensive systems generally.
problem: Misrepresents the README (A7), which says Marlin is designed for write-intensive workloads whose reads mostly touch recently written keys. The qualification is dropped, and 'right engine' is stronger than 'designed for'.

quote: Wray kept a continuous day-by-day record of the winter.
problem: Contradicted by E1: folios 31-34 are missing, and there are no entries between 12 December 1741 and 26 January 1742 (46 days). Entries are also not daily (212 over 716 days), and several were written up weeks later.

quote: The vestry responded by laying a rate for the poor, recorded on folio 38v.
problem: Unsupported causal link. The rate (fol. 38v) precedes the mill passage (fol. 39v), and nothing in the quoted passages (Q3) ties the rate to the mill stoppage or the grain shortage. 'Responded' is the summariser's inference.

quote: The parish register shows 52 burials in 1742, which is 23 more than in 1741.
problem: Arithmetic error: E5(a) gives 52 in 1742 and 33 in 1741, a rise of 19, not 23.

quote: Of the 29 death entries in the journal, Wray names a fever as the cause in seven.
problem: E5(b) says fever is named in 5 of the 29 death entries, not seven.

quote: The frost alone accounts for the rise in burials in 1742.
problem: Unsupported. Cold or frost is named in only 6 death entries and fever in 5. The rise over 1741 is 19 burials, and the journal's own entries show fever as a contributing cause, so 'alone' is not established.

quote: Wray's burial entries have been checked against the parish register and found accurate.
problem: Overstated. Q8: the editor compared only nine of Wray's burial notices (of 29 death entries) and explicitly did not check the remainder.

quote: Wray states that the vicar kept the tithe barn locked against the poor.
problem: Misrepresents Q5 (fol. 41r). Wray reports hearsay ('It is said by some'), says he has not seen it himself, and notes that Mr. Hale says the barn is empty. He does not state it as fact.

quote: The journal gives a representative picture of how rural parishes in the county fared that winter.
problem: Unsupported generalisation. E1 says the edition covers one parish and prints no records of any other parish or comparative material, so representativeness cannot be assessed.

quote: Of the 48 nurses who were screened but not randomized, most (31) declined to take part.
problem: T2 says 48 not randomized = 31 ineligible and 17 declined (ineligible reasons 19+8+4 = 31). The 31 were ineligible, not decliners.

quote: Across both arms, 56 of 64 participants (85.9%) completed the week 8 assessment.
The reduction in insomnia severity persisted after the program ended.
problem: No data support this. Assessments were at baseline and week 8 only, with none after week 8 (T1; protocol 6.3: follow-up not planned). Persistence was not measured.

quote: The sleep-restriction module is what drove the improvement.
problem: Unsupported. Components were delivered together in a fixed sequence and the study does not test individual components (T1; protocol 3.1), so no component can be credited.

quote: Engagement with the program was high.
problem: Contradicted by T5: median 5 of 8 modules (IQR 3 to 8); only 11 of 32 (34.4%) completed all 8; 8 of 32 completed 3 or fewer, including 2 who completed none. This is not high engagement.

quote: These data show the program is safe for night-shift nurses.
problem: Overclaim. Protocol 7.4 says the study is not powered to estimate adverse event rates. It was n=32 per arm with free-text self-report, collected through different channels in each arm, so 0 serious events cannot establish safety.

quote: The findings apply to shift workers generally.
problem: Overgeneralisation. A single-centre pilot of nurses at one teaching hospital with insomnia symptoms and night shifts, open-label and with exploratory efficacy outcomes, cannot support conclusions about shift workers generally.

quote: Below 3.0 kN the bracket has an effectively infinite fatigue life.
problem: Unsupported. F3: no specimen was tested below 3.0 kN, and no test was continued past the 2,000,000-cycle runout. No statistical analysis of the fatigue data was done.

quote: One of the four specimens reached the runout and the other three failed, the shortest at 1,138,000 cycles.
problem: Wrong figure: F3 and the lab log give the shortest 4.0 kN life as F4-04 at 1,238,000 cycles, not 1,138,000.

quote: At 4.0 kN the bracket has a 75 percent chance of failing before two million cycles.
problem: Unsupported inference. 3 of 4 specimens failed, but F2 says no statistical analysis of the fatigue data was performed. n=4 cannot give a 75 percent probability, and one of the failures (F4-02) was flagged as interrupted.

quote: The mean life at 5.0 kN was about 483,000 cycles.
The excess set in S08 is explained by its coming from a different material lot.
problem: Unsupported causal claim. S08 is the only lot B specimen and its mill certificate is not on file. The lab log says no sectioning, hardness or tensile tests on lot B are scheduled. Lot is confounded with a single specimen; at most it is a possible explanation.

quote: The bracket's performance carries over to the full range of service temperatures.
problem: Contradicted by F2 and F5: all tests were at laboratory ambient (20.1 to 22.6 C). REQ-EN-003 requires -30 C to +50 C, but no tests were run at other temperatures.

quote: The fatigue programme was run in accordance with ASTM E466.
problem: TP-221 says the method was only 'adapted from ASTM E466' with listed deviations: four specimens per level against a plan target of six, and load frame alignment not verified. It is not run in accordance with the standard.
